title: Project H.O.M.E.
program: Community Living, Retail, Educational, Hydroponics, Recreational Faclities
body: The built environment is a series of vast interconnected systems.

home in this case stands for housing, ownership, mentorship, and education. This project from start to finish is less about the design of the buildings, with more of a focus put into designing a system. The system, home, is an unique approach to affordable housing as a means to and end, rather than the end itself. Through housing, mentorship, and education, the goal of home is to decrease a decades long march out of poverty to less than a decade. Doing this involved rethinking the role affordable housing in America plays in the housing market. Creating a safe and affordable place for the less fortunate to live, learn, and work was the backbone of the system.

The housing space is treated more as a college dorm than an apartment, and this was necessary for several reasons. The first is affordability. By combining the kitchen, living, bathing, and study spaces, costs can be saved. Every person or family receives a private room or pair of connected rooms to live in during their time at home. By sharing the common spaces, there is the ability for them to develop important social skills that usually are learned when a young adult attends college. The people living here however are not college students, so creating a sense of community without uniformity was key to the layout of the housing blocks. After many iterations, a split level design was chosen to create what I called "a village in a building. The rooms and shared amenities are separated by an outdoor network of paths, stairs, and planted areas. This, along with space for the residents to decorate their front entryways should give the impression of a walkable neighborhood rather than an affordable housing block.

Generating income to subsidize the housing is key. Every home project will need to explore different ways to generate capital, but the key is to discover what is lacking in the surrounding built environment and cater to those needs. For this example in Mantua Philadelphia, fresh locally grown produce and lack of commercial space in the area presented great opportunities to generate wealth. By employing large amounts of indoor hydroponic farming, an astounding amount of income can be generated from the selling of goods produced at home to the surrounding city. This endeavor has the added benefit of providing additional on premise places to employ those in the program, and teach them skills in a growing urban industry. Along with the construction and renting of in demand commercial spaces and some additional small amounts of income from other operations around the site, the entire system not only pays for itself, but also has enough extra to provide social workers, teachers, and other essential recourses to those living here.

The architecture pictured above is an architectural representation of the system it is built to serve. I am intrigued by what this type of design could bring into the world. Thinking of buildings as a machine of sorts is nothing new in this profession, but doing so in a more theoretical sense while applying all we know about design today could offer very powerful solutions to problems not often associated with architecture.
